#4996. Fitbit Edge vs. Fitbit Air: Which New Fitbit Should You Buy?

Do you want a less distracting tracker or one with a screen and built-in GPS?

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

GOOGLE DIDN’T RELEASE a major new Fitbit fitness tracker for two and a half years after the Charge 6 came out in October 2023. Then it released two new models in five months. The first, the $99 Fitbit Air, came out in May and works a lot like a Whoop. You wear it day and night, and it sends your heart rate, sleep, and workout data to the Google Health app on your phone.Second is the $179 Fitbit Edge, which followed in October as the Charge 6’s successor. It offers the same features as the Air and adds a 1.34-inch screen, built-in GPS, and an ECG app that checks your heart rhythm for signs of atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that raises your stroke risk. Both trackers pair with iPhones and Android phones, so neither is exclusive to Google’s platform.For most people, deciding between them comes down to one question: do you want to see your pace and heart rate on your wrist during a workout, or are you fine checking everything on your phone afterward?

With no screen and no buttons, the Fitbit Air is as simple as they come to use. Google rates its battery at up to seven days, so you won’t have to charge every night. It’s also the cheaper way to get Google’s Health Coach. The $99 price includes three free months of Google’s Health Premium, which costs $9.99 a month after that.The Fitbit Edge shows your pace and heart rate on its screen during a workout, and its built-in GPS records your route without your phone. If you run or ride outdoors, you can leave your phone at home and still come back with a map and split times. The Edge also has two sensors the Air doesn’t: electrical sensors for the ECG app, and an altimeter that measures elevation gain on a hike and counts the floors you climb. It costs $80 more than the Air, and turning on its always-on display cuts the battery from about seven days to about two.

The Air’s tracker module is a 1.37 x 0.66-inch pod, and it’s about 25 percent smaller than the discontinued Fitbit Luxe. The pod pops out of its band and snaps into another one in a few seconds, so you can wear the fabric Performance Loop to sleep and switch to the silicone Active Band for a sweaty workout. If you want something dressier, the polyurethane Elevated Modern Band and a new Metal Mesh band are also available.The Edge measures 1.54 x 1.01 inches and is almost half an inch thick, with a pill-shaped body that’s noticeably larger than the Air. A side button opens the app list and takes you back to the clock face. It comes in Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon, with six band styles that run from the sweat-resistant Active Sport Band to a Metal Links bracelet. Both trackers are rated IP68 and 5ATM, which means they have dust and water protection.

The Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge record the same health data. Both measure your heart rate around the clock, plus blood oxygen, overnight skin temperature changes, and heart rate variability (HRV), the variation in time between heartbeats. HRV usually drops when you’re stressed, sick, or haven’t recovered from hard training.The Google Health app uses those readings to set a Readiness score each morning. It also tracks Cardio Load, which estimates how much cardiovascular strain your workouts create, while your personalized weekly target helps you balance activity and recovery. It can help you spot changes in your training load, but it can’t tell you exactly what your body can handle. Both trackers can alert you to an irregular rhythm that could be atrial fibrillation. They can also notify you when your heart rate stays unusually high or low while you’re inactive. Both also have Smart Wake, which vibrates to wake you during light sleep inside a time window you set.The Edge adds a few health tools the Air doesn’t have. Its ECG app records your heart’s electrical activity whenever you start a reading. If your heart feels like it’s racing or skipping, you can take a reading in the moment and save it to show your doctor. The Edge has a dedicated skin-temperature sensor, while older Fitbits such as the Charge 6 use a device-temperature sensor to track overnight skin-temperature variation.With Google Health Premium, both trackers get Google’s advanced Health Guardian features, which track trends in your blood pressure and insulin resistance. Google says they aren’t meant to screen or diagnose any condition.Both trackers start logging common workouts on their own. In my testing, the Air logged walks and lifting sessions without my starting them. Google says an update expands automatic detection on both the Air and Edge from 10 workout types to more than 100, including strength training, swimming, and racket sports. A workout only gets logged automatically if it lasts at least 15 minutes and keeps your heart rate up, so you may have to log short or stop-and-start sessions yourself.

The Fitbit Edge has built-in GPS, so it can map your route and measure your pace and distance without your phone. Google says the Edge’s GPS is up to 40 percent more accurate than its earlier trackers, thanks to a new GPS chip and case design. The Edge also has an altimeter, which reads air pressure to measure how much elevation you gain on a hilly run or how many floors you climb on a stair workout.The Edge’s screen also shows your stats during a workout, giving you instant feedback. You can set a pace target before a run and check on the screen whether you’re ahead of pace or lagging behind. During HIIT intervals, you can see which heart rate zone you’re in. On the track, it shows your split for each lap.The Fitbit Air has no GPS and no screen. To map a run, you have to carry your phone, and you can’t check your pace or heart rate until you look at the Google Health app afterward. If you mostly lift or walk and don’t want instant feedback, the Air is a great option. But if you care about your splits, the Edge is the better tracker.

The Fitbit Edge comes with nine apps, including Google Maps, Weather, and Timer. You can’t download more, and unlike the Pixel Watch 5, it doesn’t let you talk to Gemini from your wrist. Google Maps shows turn-by-turn directions on the Edge only after you start navigation on your phone, so you can’t look up a destination on the tracker itself.Calls and texts from your phone show up on the Edge’s screen. On Android, you can answer a text with a preset reply like “on my way.” Those quick replies don’t work with an iPhone, so iPhone owners can read texts on the Edge but have to answer them on the phone. Swiping down on the Edge opens a control panel where you can turn on Do Not Disturb, use the screen as a flashlight, or make your phone ring when you can’t find it.The Fitbit Air has none of this. Its only feature you’ll notice day to day is the Smart Wake alarm, which vibrates to wake you up. Everything else, including the Health Coach, lives in the Google Health app, which also syncs with Apple Health if you want your data in one place on an iPhone.Neither tracker has NFC, so you can’t use either one to pay with Google Wallet.

You don’t need a subscription to use either tracker. Without one, the Google Health app still shows your steps, heart rate, HRV, blood oxygen, sleep score and stages, Readiness, Cardio Load, and workouts. It also alerts you to an irregular heart rhythm. Google Health Premium costs $9.99 a month, and the Air and Edge each come with three months free.Premium adds the Gemini-powered Health Coach, which you can message anytime with questions about your data, plus weekly workout plans that adjust to your schedule. When I told it my shoulder was sore, it reworked that week’s plan around it. It also adds more detailed sleep summaries, meal logging from a photo, and plain-language summaries of your lab results.

The Charge 6 came out in 2023 and retails for $159.95. It has an ECG app and built-in GPS, and it can track more than 40 types of exercise. The Fitbit Edge improves on almost all of that. Its screen is 46 percent bigger, it’s rated IP68 for dust resistance, and it charges in about 90 minutes instead of two hours. And when the Edge’s battery wears out, you can replace it yourself instead of buying a new tracker.The Edge does drop two features the Charge 6 offers. The first is NFC, the chip that lets you pay with Google Wallet. The second is the EDA Scan app, which measures small changes in the sweat on your skin to estimate your stress level. If you’re buying a new tracker, the Charge 6 makes sense only if you pay with your wrist or find it well below the Edge’s $179 price (it’s down to $129.95 on Google’s site at the time of publication).The Fitbit Inspire 3 is the cheapest Fitbit with a screen, at about $100. It’s smaller than the Charge 6, lasts longer between charges, and starts tracking walks and runs automatically. It has no GPS or ECG, but it remains a solid choice if you want to see the time and your step count on your wrist without paying for the Edge.

Buy the Fitbit Air if you lift, walk, or take classes and mostly want to know how well you slept and how hard to train each day. At $99, it gets you the same heart rate, HRV, and sleep data as the Edge, and the same Health Coach if you pay for Premium. Because it has no screen, nothing on your wrist lights up or buzzes during dinner or in the middle of the night.For $80 more than the Air, the Edge gets you built-in GPS that maps your route and measures your pace without your phone. The screen shows your splits and heart rate zones while you’re moving, and the altimeter counts the elevation you climb. The ECG app also lets you check your heart rhythm the moment something feels off.If you already have a Charge 6, you don’t have to upgrade to get Google’s newest software. The Health Coach and Premium features come through the Google Health app, so they work on the tracker you already own. Upgrade to the Edge if the Charge 6’s battery no longer gets you through the week. But it’s worth keeping if you pay with your wrist. Neither new Fitbit has NFC, so the Charge 6 is the only one of the three that works with Google Wallet.

Two weeks ago, The New York Times reported that Nvidia’s CEO had a close relationship with an executive at a Singapore chip buyer under US export-control investigation. Things escalated quickly from there.

On Sunday, Jensen Huang told employees he had been unfaithful to his wife of 40 years, and Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. On Wednesday, The Times reported a second relationship, this one with an executive who reports directly to him. Three Republican committee chairs were preparing a subpoena.

Thursday morning he resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. The company gave no reason.

CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO while keeping the CFO job. She has been Nvidia’s finance chief since 2013, through the entire AI buildout, and spent 13 years at Microsoft before that. The board also named Harvey Jones, formerly of Synopsys, as its first-ever chair, and started a search that will consider internal and external candidates with no timeline attached.

The stock fell as much as 14% before recovering to close down about 4%. Nvidia has now shed more than a trillion dollars in market value this month.

Bitcoin fell roughly 4% to a twelve-week low near $68,000, down from above $76,000 earlier in the week. ETH lost about 3% and is now below $2,000. Solana, BNB and XRP all fell between 3% and 5%. The broad market index was off about 4% on the day and 7% on the week.

It’s a bleak picture. But there are some local reasons for hope.

Second, Binance reported Thursday afternoon that it has completed coverage of the assets affected by its $6.34 billion hack and published an expanded Proof of Reserves snapshot covering all 44 cryptocurrencies impacted. Many believe that the Binance post-hack aftermath has been weighing on crypto prices, and now perhaps this coverage will help alleviate some pain.

And then Nvidia reports fiscal Q3 results on Tuesday. Any positive news about Jensen succession planning, the Q3 results and/or future growth will likely stop the bleeding on one of the biggest assets across markets (also helping crypto most likely).

We will find out soon if it’s enough to stop the bleeding…

Hyperliquid’s Q3 revenue rose 22% to $191 million as daily traders hit a record and stock-linked trading volumes surged.

Hyperliquid closed out the third quarter with a record $16.8 billion in open derivatives positions following a July slowdown.

Open interest jumped nearly 80% from the end of June, according to a new report from the Hyperliquid Research Collective. This was enough for Hyperliquid to surpass centralized exchange rivals Bybit, Kraken and OKX in open interest.

Its share of open interest across Hyperliquid and eight major exchanges climbed to 11.7%, up from 9.6% three months earlier.

Wintermute, one of crypto's biggest market makers, has become a major user of Hyperliquid's auctions for early access to trading data, Bloomberg reported Thursday.

A wallet linked to Wintermute won 76% of auctions for the top-priority data slot over the preceding month, according to analysis from Loris Tools and cited by Bloomberg.

#4990. The 7 Best Body Groomers for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Trimmers and shavers for everywhere below the neck.

LIKE EVERYTHING ELSE, body grooming trends come and go. Just look at the wild, hairy 1970s or the Ken doll slick early aughts if you don’t believe me. Right now, we are living in what I would argue is the golden age of body hair. As in, you can do whatever you want with it. You can trim! You can wax! You can let it grow… and grow… and grow!

But the reality is that most men (at least 62 percent) do something to their body hair. This isn’t to say that you’re required to manscape, but whether you already do or you’re about to give it a try for the first time, the most important thing in any manscaping journey is the tool you use.

Anyone who has shaved even once knows that the risk of cutting and nicking skin is very real, especially when you get down to very sensitive or hard-to-reach areas. Trimming, whether it's using hair clippers or electric razors, has its own set of headaches in the form of pulling hairs and not having enough protection between the blade and your skin.

That’s where the best body groomers come in—they’re specifically designed to be gentle on sensitive areas (like your twig and berries) and make the grooming experience way more pleasant. And before you ask why you need another tool for this job, consider this: Using the same razor or trimmer on your body as you do on your face can lead to bacterial cross-contamination. Do you really want jock itch on your chin?

These days, body and pubic trimmers are technologically advanced to help make the job way easier. We’re talking long-lasting charges, waterproof casings, multiple guards, special blades, and more. So whatever hair you’re hoping to tackle, and no matter how much of it you have, the best body groomers will get the job done quickly and comfortably.

Throughout our testing of over 50 body groomers, we found that Panasonic's GK80 is the best in class. There’s a lot to love about this groomer. The unique V-shaped blade and ergonomic design allow you to trim even the hardest-to-reach crevices with ease, and the innovative length guard oscillates between 12 different lengths with the turn of a dial, so you never have to take it off while switching lengths. It delivers one of the most customizable and easiest experiences you could hope for in a body trimmer.

What Else to Consider: The innovative design of this groomer is what sets it apart, but it still takes a bit of a learning curve to figure out the best way to use it on your body. It doesn’t follow the traditional push vs. pull methods that most trimmers do. Because of the V-shaped blade, it’s able to cut in both directions, which does make it easier, but if you’re switching from using a more traditional groomer, it can feel weird at first. The adjustable trimmer head is effective, but also bulky and may take some practice getting used to.

It’s convenient to avoid completely switching combs in the middle of a trimming session, but it can also make the trimmer feel a little top-heavy, and some of our testers found it reduces the effectiveness of the blades. The rinse-to-clean capability is great, but we’d advise using it dry instead of wet (that goes for pretty much all of these trimmers, to be honest).

Why We Chose It: For sheer ease of use, the Panasonic Body Groomer GK80 cannot be beat. The innovative design, multi-directional cutting capability, adjustable dial length comb, and V-shaped head all combine to make this easily the most intuitive and efficient body groomer available. Sure, it’s not perfect—it’s slightly better at shaving than trimming, for instance—but its pros exceed its cons by a landslide.

We found in our testing that using it dry is more effective, but it’s just as comfortable shaving your more sensitive groin areas as it is for the chest, arms, and shoulders. And while it is on the expensive side, if you groom or trim your body hair regularly, it’s a solid investment.

Long-Term Testing Notes: We’ve been using this device for over two years, and the effectiveness of the Body Groomer GK80 has not waned. What we have noticed, however, is that it's better for shaving than trimming. Not that it does a bad job; it’s just that the shaving capability is better than the other trimmers in our arsenal (save for perhaps the Philips Norelco OneBlade), while the trimming capabilities with the adjustable comb are comparable to some others. Still, it remains our go-to trimmer because of how comfortable it is to hold and how nimble it is at cutting hair in hard-to-reach places, thanks to the wand design.Read More: Panasonic GK80 Review

Whether you want to mow the lawn completely or just give it a little trim, this groomer does it all. With multiple-length combs and ceramic blades that are gentle on even your most sensitive areas, this is one of the most effective body groomers out there.

What Else to Consider: This is a classic push-style trimmer, which means you push it toward you (usually against the grain) to cut the hair. This is not a bad thing, just good to know going into the purchase, in case you are used to a pull-style trimmer. Why We Chose It: If you’re a consistent trimmer of your undercarriage, the Manscaper 5.0 is one of the best tools out there to get the job done effectively. We also love the additional features that many of the other groomers on this list don’t have, like a wireless charging dock and LED spotlight (it may seem gimmicky at first, but trust us, it helps). Long-Term Testing Notes: Months after first testing the Manscaper 5.0, we still go back to it for specific areas of our bodies, namely the undercarriage. Make sure you give yourself adequate time to use it slowly, or the risk of nicks and cuts increases exponentially.

If you’re into streamlining, this all-in-one trimmer does everything: your hair, your beard, and your body (just make sure to clean it before switching locations—it’s fully washable). What Else to Consider: Using a clipper for everything is convenient, but it requires some adjusting of your technique depending on where you use it. This multipurpose groomer is optimized for cutting the hair on your head, so it’s powerful—more powerful than some of the other dedicated body groomers on this list.

That means proceed with caution when taking it downstairs to more sensitive areas. Use it with a guard to get the hang of it and avoid nicks and cuts on your tender bits in the process. You’ll also want to thoroughly clean it before using it on your head or beard to avoid cross-contamination.

Why We Chose It: As far as multipurpose groomers go, the Philips Norelco Multigroomer is top-of-the-line. We love that it’s hefty and durable and feels more like a traditional hair clipper than anything else. Also, we found that it’s incredibly powerful and can cut through even thick, coarse hair with ease.

You also can’t beat the options you get with 18 different attachments. It’s able to do any cutting, trimming, or detailing you could possibly want. It truly is an all-in-one tool ready to attack whatever you throw at it.

Long-Term Testing Notes: Even after the testing phase, the Philips Norelco Multigroomer continues to be one of our go-to tools for trimming and cutting hair. But we find ourselves reaching for it more as a hair clipper and beard trimmer than a full-on body groomer.

We tend to use it more on less-sensitive areas like our chests. And when it comes time to trim below the belt, we reach for something a little more gentle. That said, it’s still well worth the investment if you don’t want to clutter your bathroom with multiple tools.

Don't worry if you're not flexible: This handy tool lets you reach all areas of your back by yourself. An added Power Burst button shaves through extra-thick and coarse hair.

What Else to Consider: Shaving your back is hard to achieve on your own with a traditional body groomer—it’s usually a two-person job. The long, angled arm of this shaver is specifically designed to allow you to fully shave your back without help.

There are two heads, but they are both shavers—one is just wider than the other to cover more surface area. There aren’t any length attachments here because of the assumption that most guys want to completely shave their backs, and that’s probably true.

Like with any trimmer, there is a slight learning curve to using it, but especially this one, as it still takes some dexterity to understand where you are shaving and to see your progress in the mirror. It’s also not designed to shave or trim other parts of your body because of the bulky, angled arm. It’s not for everyone, but if you regularly shave your back (or have someone else do it for you), it could be worth the investment.

Why We Chose It: We’ll say it again, we are always fans of using the best tool for whatever job you’re doing. Back shaving is incredibly tough to do on your own, so anything that helps make that process easier is great in our book. It’s relatively simple to use and isn’t bogged down with extra functions to confuse the process. Once you get the hang of it, it’s an important tool in your body grooming arsenal if your back is a focal point for you.

Long-Term Testing Notes: Over a year of using this tool, its battery life still holds up for hours. That being said, we have had to replace the foil (totally expected once you pass the year mark). But once the blades started to dull, we found them to be more prone to hair pulling.

Not only do the stainless steel blades cut through even the coarsest hair, but the rounded, wraparound guards protect your junk from nicks and cuts. The integrated dial allows a whopping 39 (!) different cutting lengths for a truly customized experience. Plus, it’s completely waterproof and has a 100-minute run time on a single charge.

What Else to Consider: If you’re a fan of trimming in the shower, this option is one of the best for wet use. We found that it's completely waterproof, which makes shower shaving a breeze, not to mention cleanup. Just keep in mind that, in general, wet trimming is slightly more difficult than dry trimming—but of course, you can’t beat that cleanup.

The wraparound guard design makes it less harrowing to trim your sensitive areas, but it won’t give you the closest shave. For that, you’ll have to take it off, which is still comfortable, but more prone to nicks and cuts. And if you’re a frequent traveler who likes to trim on the go, the travel lock is important since it doesn’t come with a case.

Why We Chose It: For a more inexpensive trimmer, this one still has all the features you want, like a quick charge option, wet/dry functionality, and a variety of lengths. Not to mention, some that you didn’t know you wanted, but once you try, you’ll love, like the rotary dial to adjust trimming length easily without needing to switch combs.

Overall, this groomer is reliable and versatile, and while the blades are not quite as sharp as more premium models, it still gets the job done when you need it to.

Long-Term Testing Notes: After a year of use, the Wahl Manscaper is still able to handle whatever hair we throw at it without a struggle. That being said, while it remains usable in water, we have found that 100-minute battery life to be more like 90 minutes—though that's still longer than most other options available.

In general, body hair is thicker than facial hair, so you'll need devices that have more power than your typical electric razor. That said, we suggest looking for a tool with an extensive battery life, so you'll spend less time charging and more time shaving. In our experience, that's something with at least 40 minutes or more of runtime. The groomers we've selected as the best have battery lives that extend from 40 minutes to six hours.

Manscaping during or directly after showering can make the whole process much more seamless, with less risk of nicks or pulling. For this, you'll want to check out options that are water-resistant to ensure you can use them while you take a shower or right after you hop out. This will also assist in the cleaning process, as you can simply run the tool under water and leave everything out until it dries.

Every trimmer on this list is electric, which means they have one of two blade types: rotary or foil. In general, the biggest difference between the two is that rotary blades cut hair in a circular motion while foil blades cut in one direction, essentially up and down or side to side. Foils also typically cut closer, but rotary blades are more adept at maneuvering the contours of the body. That being said, rotary blades are better at attacking thicker or coarser hair, while foils are often more gentle on sensitive skin. So it really comes down to what you value more.

When it comes to electric grooming devices, chargers have come a long way from their battery-powered origins (although there are still plenty of these options around for those who prefer them). The two main alternatives to batteries are a cord or plug directly connecting the tool to an outlet and a stand that charges the groomer while it's mounted. Neither is necessarily better than the other (including the battery-powered); it mostly comes down to personal preference.

That being said, depending on your bathroom setup, you may want to zero in on certain options. For those with limited counter or storage space, you’ll probably want to opt for a plug that you can charge when needed and then store when not in use. But if you have the counter space, a charging mount can be super convenient and help keep your device sufficiently charged at all times.

Body hair can differ significantly in prevalence, thickness, and sensitivity from one area to another. With this in mind, many devices will include multiple blades meant specifically for various areas of the body. This also helps from a hygiene standpoint, as you wouldn’t want to reuse the same blade for every crevice of the body to avoid cross-contamination between different zones.

Just as different parts of your body require different blades, you probably won’t want every area to maintain the same length of hair. For example, you may want your back to be as bald as possible, but probably not your chest (unless you’re a competitive swimmer or bodybuilder). For this, varying attachments that offer different desired lengths can be super helpful, especially if you’re someone who does widespread body grooming.

If you’re anything like us, you value organization when it comes to your grooming arsenal. It makes sense; the more tools and products you have, the more space they’ll take up, and the more likely you are to lose track of attachments, cords, and anything else that’s not directly connected to your device. This is where a case can really be crucial to help hold all of your body groomer’s attachments and gadgets in one convenient place.

For the past three years, Men's Health's grooming editors and writers have done extensive research and testing for body groomers. Throughout this time, we have tested over 50 body groomers (both wet and dry) for extended periods of time, evaluating all the picks on effectiveness, safety, comfort, ease of use, reliability, battery life, and value. From there, we then trimmed (get it?) the list down to the seven best body groomers for men that are worth your money.

#4989. CFTC’s Selig accuses states of trying to ‘lock up’ prediction market founders

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Chair Michael Selig defends federal oversight of prediction markets as states pursue enforcement and the CFTC presses its authority in court.

Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig is turning up the heat on his criticisms of states' handling of lawsuits brought against prediction market platforms and their executives.

Speaking at the Cantor Convergence conference, Selig called the state suits "really egregious" and defended the platforms operating under what he has long called the CFTC's "exclusive jurisdiction."

"We're seeing states bring criminal charges, essentially trying to lock up founders and CEOs of these companies that are offering lawful products under a federal regime," he said.

The comments come amid a stretch of battles between the CFTC and roughly a dozen states and cities over whether event contracts offered on prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket constitute illegal gambling. Selig argued that the disagreements should be hashed out in court without threatening executives with time in prison.

"Somebody says it's gambling, somebody says it's a derivative," he said. "That's not something that should be at the risk of going to jail."

And instead of fighting on a case-by-case basis in multiple states, Selig wants to see the issue raised to the Supreme Court in a bid to solidify the CFTC's authority.

"I don't understand whether we're going to have every major CEO of an exchange locked up in a jail cell in Utah, or if we can just go to the Supreme Court and hash this thing out on the merits," he said.

On Thursday, the Justice Department and CFTC sued Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin to block his action against Kalshi.

Louisiana also filed a lawsuit Thursday targeting companies including Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood and Coinbase.

"I am concerned that some of the states are getting very aggressive," Selig said. "We’ll continue to defend our jurisdiction."

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On Friday, the committee released its findings of an investigation it launched in May on insider trading risks in prediction markets among government officials.

The Republican chair of the House Oversight Committee is calling for new limits on government officials' use of prediction markets, including the possibility of an outright ban, amid growing concerns that public officials could use insider information to profit from bets on the platforms.

On Friday, the committee released findings from an investigation it launched in May into insider trading risks in prediction markets among government officials, military personnel, and those with security clearances. The committee sifted through 1,700 pages of documents and also received five bipartisan staff briefings from prediction market companies, said Chair James Comer, R-Ky.

Concerns in Washington have intensified over the past year, particularly after an active-duty U.S. Army soldier who used confidential information to place bets on Polymarket ahead of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro's capture. Thereafter, others in government have also been found using inside information to make money on bets on prediction markets, including the White House's former teleprompter operator. Political candidates have also faced allegations of insider trading on the platforms.

"Congress must consider additional reforms to prevent public corruption and restore the American people's trust in government," Comer said on Friday.

Those reforms should be legislation that restricts which bets federal employees, lawmakers and congressional staff can place on prediction markets — or an outright ban, the committee said.

"Whether it's an outright prohibition on trading on prediction markets or restrictions on some subset of contracts like government-related contracts, applying these restrictions to officials in all branches of government would strengthen ethical expectations that government personnel should not personally and financially benefit from access to non-public information associated with their work as government servants…" according to the memo.

Congress should also have a role in encouraging prediction market companies and federal agencies to share necessary information to enforce restrictions, the committee said.

Both major prediction market companies — Kalshi and Polymarket — have said they have taken steps to tighten controls to prevent government officials from using inside information. Lawmakers have also begun addressing the issue themselves. In April, the Senate voted to pass a resolution to ban members from trading on prediction markets.

#4984. ‘Roadmap is Complete,' Cardano Founder Charles Hoskinson Says

‘Roadmap is Complete,' Cardano Founder Charles Hoskinson Says

Charles Hoskinson said that the Cardano "roadmap is complete" and that everything he said would be built has finished. It came during a YouTube livestream Saturday where Hoskinson sparred with disgruntled investors as ADA sits down 94% from its 2021 high, per Decrypt data.

One viewer, named shevilkid1738, pushed Hoskinson's buttons by claiming he'd promised Cardano would overtake Bitcoin. The Cardano founder clapped back, saying there was no evidence he ever said that.

"I never promised that. I said I'd love for it to happen, and I believe that Cardano is a better store of value than Bitcoin is for a variety of reasons," Hoskinson said. "I don't promise price appreciation, or people overturning things. I say it's absolutely possible."

Shevilkid1738 responded over an hour later with a quote where Hoskinson said he "thinks" Cardano is "probably" going to become the biggest cryptocurrency in the world. Hoskinson highlighted the word think and said that he has "taken it as far as I can," explaining that the network is now decentralized and doesn't rely on him as a founder.

The viewer wasn't happy and called it "insane" for a founder to no longer have a responsibility to those who invested in their project.

"Under what conditions does that obligation end?" Hoskinson said, "The roadmap is complete. Everything I said is going to be built has been built. It reached four times the value of Honda. There's millions of people that have used it, and millions of people continue to use it. It is self-determining and self-governing, with its ability to pick and choose its own leaders without my consent."

Cardano’s roadmap was split into five eras: Byron, Shelly, Goguen, Basho, and Voltaire.

Byron launched the network in September 2017, Shelley added staking in July 2020, and Goguen brought smart contracts via the Alonzo hard fork in September 2021. Basho, the scaling era, came via the Vasil upgrade in September 2022, before the Chang hard fork kicked off Voltaire, the governance era, in September 2024.

The final piece to the puzzle occurred in January 2025, when the Plomin hard fork gave ADA holders "real voting power" over the blockchain’s future. This marked the transition to "full decentralized governance," and apparently the end of the final roadmap era.

"The goal was simple. There's a roadmap. Byron, Basho, Shelley, et cetera, et cetera, and it's done," Hoskinson said. "I have no power over this ecosystem."

Ultimately, though, Hoskinson says the issue that investors have is financial.

"You want me to pump your bags. That's what you're really saying. The job's not done till it's pumped," he said. "But guess what? It's never done then, because somebody comes in at $3 ADA, and then expects it to be five. And then somebody comes in at $5 ADA and expects it to be seven. If you retire at five, you've defrauded the person at five. If you retire at three, you've defrauded the person at three. There's no winning."

ADA hit an all-time high of $3.09 in 2021 and has been on a downward slide ever since. By 2023, it hit a low of $0.25 before pumping 384% to a high of $1.21 by the end of 2024. Since then, its price has tanked 86% to $0.17.

"Apparently, I have to go pump your bags, and if I don't, I'm a scammer," Hoskinson said. "Would you sign up for that deal? Would any human being sign up for that? I thought slavery was made illegal."

#4983. Bitcoin Price Falls 14% in a Week to $65,000 as Weekend Selling Breaks Friday’s Low

Bitcoin price crashed about 13% over the past week and traded near $65,600 on Saturday.

Bitcoin price crashed about 14% over the past week and was trading near $65,200 on Saturday morning after sliding to about $65,000, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data. The move broke below Friday’s low of about $67,555 and marked the weakest level since mid-August, as weekend trading extended a selloff that has followed a stronger dollar and a fully priced December Federal Reserve rate hike.

A week ago, on Nov. 7, bitcoin was trading near $75,750. The decline steepened after Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, a shake-up that caused AI stocks to sell off which could potentially be responsible for sending bitcoin below $72,000. It slipped toward $71,000 by Thursday evening, then crashed to about $67,555 around midnight Eastern on Friday, its lowest level since August, before recovering toward $69,800 in the morning.

A brief pop above $70,000 after the producer-price report faded, and the bitcoin price spent Friday afternoon pinned below $70,000, near $68,900.

Selling resumed Friday evening and carried into the mid-$66,000s. Bitcoin briefly steadied overnight near $67,000, then sold off again after 8 a.m. ET Saturday, reaching that $65,500 low in the 10 a.m. hour and taking out Friday’s trough.

The Labor Department said Friday that the Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3% in October, short of the 0.4% increase economists had expected. On an unadjusted basis, the index was up 6.5% from a year earlier, the largest 12-month rise since November 2022. The slightly cooler monthly figure lifted bitcoin above $70,000 for only minutes.

Bond traders were unconvinced. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed as high as 5.17% on Friday, a four-week high, and closed at 5.15%. The U.S. dollar index held at a 19-month high, its strongest level since April 2025. Boston Fed President Susan Collins said Friday that “soon, some additional tightening of Fed monetary policy may be appropriate,” and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said policymakers will, “in all likelihood, raise interest rates.” Higher rates raise the cost of holding an asset that pays no interest, and a stronger dollar has weighed on the bitcoin price for much of November. Traders fully priced a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting, CME FedWatch data show.

Chip stocks offered no cushion. The iShares Semiconductor ETF fell more than 3% on Friday, and Advanced Micro Devices dropped more than 8%. The Nasdaq 100 closed down 1.22%. U.S. stock and bond markets are closed Saturday, but those levels still frame the weekend session. Nvidia is due to report third-quarter results on Tuesday under interim CEO Colette Kress, the first earnings release since Huang stepped down.

Demand from spot bitcoin ETFs has not filled the gap. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) bled $2 billion over nine straight days of outflows through Wednesday, and the funds posted a sixth straight day of net outflows on Thursday. Weekend trading is typically thinner, leaving the bitcoin price more exposed to sharp swings in either direction.

Miners got some relief overnight. Bitcoin’s mining difficulty dropped 9.13% at 12:02 a.m. ET Saturday at block 975,744, falling from about 148.36 trillion to 134.82 trillion, the largest cut since June. Difficulty adjusts automatically every 2,016 blocks to keep average block times near 10 minutes.

The next tests for the bitcoin price arrive quickly. Traders will watch whether Saturday’s slide holds below Friday’s $67,555 low, and whether Nvidia’s report on Tuesday extends the chip-stock weakness that has followed bitcoin lower all week. With a December rate hike fully priced and the dollar at a 19-month high, any further jump in yields when markets reopen could keep pressure on.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $65,100.

Meta’s employee trial advances its prediction market push as Kalshi and Polymarket battle state gambling lawsuits.

Meta has started internal testing of a prediction market app with its employees that would let users compete on guessing the outcome of events without putting real money on the line, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday.

The app, now going by the name Takes, lets users bet "cred" points, according to the report, which cited people familiar with the matter. Similar to other mainstream prediction markets that use money, correct predictions on Takes earn cred while wrong ones lose points.

The testing phase follows June reports that CEO Mark Zuckerberg directed employees to build a standalone prediction market app that would use points, though Meta had not ruled out eventually allowing real-money betting. At the time, the app was going by the name Arena.

The Journal's report does not say whether real-money contracts remain a possibility. Meta declined to comment or give a timetable for a public release.

It comes as real-money platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket are facing lawsuits from states that accuse them of offering illegal gambling. The platforms maintain that their event contracts are legal and fall under the jurisdiction of the federal government.

Speaking at the Cantor Convergence conference on Friday, Commodity and Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig criticized states for pursuing criminal charges against prediction market executives, adding that the disputes should be raised to the Supreme Court.

"Somebody says it's gambling, somebody says it’s a derivative," Selig said. "That's not something that should be at the risk of going to jail."

#4976. Crypto Laundering a 'Material Risk' for UK Ahead of FATF Review: RUSI

Crypto Laundering a 'Material Risk' for UK Ahead of FATF Review: RUSI

Britain's new crypto rules will still be in transition when global anti-money laundering assessors arrive next year, and the country will be judged on whether it can enforce against crypto laundering, a taskforce convened by the Royal United Services Institute has warned.

The report, published on Friday, sets out the issues the London-based defense and security think tank's taskforce expects to dominate the UK's 2027 evaluation by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). The Paris-based body sets global standards against money laundering and terrorist financing, and its peer reviews, known as mutual evaluations, grade countries on whether their rules work in practice.

The UK's report is due to be agreed at FATF's February 2028 plenary. The taskforce, made up of experts from the private sector, law enforcement and civil society, met in September; its discussions are not attributed to individual members.

This will be the first UK evaluation in which FATF considers crypto, and the taskforce was clear that crypto is a "material risk" for the UK. The City of London Police assesses that 66% of investment fraud in the UK involves crypto, according to the report, while the UK's 2025 National Risk Assessment rated crypto money laundering high risk, up from medium in 2020.

The UK brought crypto firms under its money laundering rules in 2020, and legislation passed in February created a statutory crypto regime. The Financial Conduct Authority set out which crypto activities it will regulate in April and finalized its rulebook in June, but the mandatory regime does not take effect until October 25, 2027.

The taskforce doubted the UK would be able to show adequate implementation by the time FATF visits in June, and said the UK had moved more conservatively than Hong Kong, the EU and Singapore.

Members were unanimous that assessors would examine this, and pointed to over-the-counter brokers, which the National Crime Agency estimated in the 2025 risk assessment are likely to launder hundreds of millions of dollars a year.

The taskforce cited the Metropolitan Police's £5.5 billion (about $7.3 billion) crypto seizure, linked to a Chinese professional money launderer sentenced in 2025, as an encouraging sign of what the UK criminal justice system can do when it has the capacity. But one member said the success had not been repeated in enough cases, and that the UK had barely scratched the surface of crypto laundering. FATF is expected to test whether results match the risk rather than rest on one headline case, the report said.

It also warned that because the UK's regime, which resembles the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, focuses on identifiable crypto firms, it risks pushing the highest-risk crypto outside the FCA's perimeter. That would leave law enforcement to trace assets the regulator cannot reach, such as Tether's USDT, with the taskforce pointing to a July 2025 Treasury report that flagged the stablecoin as having been "extensively exploited" by Russian-speaking laundering networks. Members doubted law enforcement had been given the capability and resources to keep pace.

The taskforce did praise UK international cooperation, including Operation Destabilise, which targeted Russian-speaking networks converting street cash into crypto. But it flagged resourcing of the UK Financial Intelligence Unit and law enforcement's economic crime capacity as likely vulnerabilities.

FATF has been pressing countries on crypto enforcement more broadly. In July, it said nearly 93% of jurisdictions it surveyed had yet to apply its standards to qualifying DeFiplatforms.

#4971. Bitcoin Hits 12-Week Low as Fed Rate Fears Undo Most of Summer Rally

Bitcoin Hits 12-Week Low as Fed Rate Fears Undo Most of Summer Rally

Bitcoin fell to roughly $68,500 on Friday, hitting its lowest price in 12 weeks as renewed U.S. inflation worries and investor withdrawals pushed the cryptocurrency further into the red.

BTC was down about 4.5% over 24 hours and 9.5% for the week, according to Friday market data. Ethereum traded near $1,925, while Solana slipped below $80 as selling spread across major cryptocurrencies.

The latest slide has erased most of Bitcoin's late-summer recovery. But not all of it: BTC remains approximately 16% above its late-June low near $59,000, even after retreating roughly 21% from its autumn peak around $86,000.

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee warned Friday that inflation had spread beyond energy and tariffs, with rising services and medical costs and demand from AI data centers adding to price pressures.

“Are we on a path back to 2%? My feeling right now is we are not and we've got to deal with that,” Goolsbee said according to Reuters.

Goolsbee did not explicitly endorse a December rate hike. But other Fed officials have been more direct.

On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he supported raising interest rates by at least 25 basis points, or 0.25 percentage points, at the December 8-9 meeting.

He also established a threshold for considering something more aggressive.

“If the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed,” Waller said in his official remarks.

The report subsequently showed core CPI rising exactly 0.3%, exceeding the 0.2% forecast and meeting Waller's condition for considering a 50-basis-point increase.

Markets have responded accordingly. Futures-based rate probabilities as of November 13 showed a 91.9% probability of a quarter-point increase and an 8.1% probability of a half-point increase.

Those figures reflect trader expectations, not a decision by the Fed. The central bank's current target range is 3.75% to 4.00%.

Friday's producer-price report added to the concerns. Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, less than forecast, but increased 6.5% year over year, the largest annual jump since 2022.

For Bitcoin, higher rates make traditional interest-bearing investments relatively more attractive, reducing the appeal of speculative assets.

Meanwhile, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have registered six consecutive sessions of net outflows, totaling approximately $1.49 billion between November 5 and November 12.

Thursday's $47.7 million withdrawal extended the five-day outflow streak, bringing another source of pressure to an already struggling market.

That does not mean institutional investors have abandoned Bitcoin. The funds still hold approximately $55.5 billion in cumulative net inflows, but it does show the state of nervousness that investors are feeling.

Weakening ETF demand, combined with forced liquidations of leveraged traders, can accelerate a decline when buyers are scarce.

Bitcoin's daily chart now shows a clear sequence of lower highs and lower lows, confirming a bearish short-term trajectory.

Its relative strength index, or RSI, has dropped to 25.4. Readings below 30 are generally considered oversold, suggesting the selling may be stretched.The average directional index, or ADX, stands at 25.3, indicating an established trend. Combined with declining prices, that suggests bearish momentum remains meaningful.

There is still one longer-term positive signal: the 50-day exponential moving average remains above the 200-day EMA, preserving a bullish moving-average configuration. But Bitcoin's price has fallen below the shorter-term average, indicating that recent momentum has turned against buyers.

Immediate support sits around $67,650, Friday's intraday low. Losing that level could expose a deeper support area near $64,000.

On the upside, Bitcoin needs to recover $70,815 and $72,775 before challenging the stronger resistance zone between $74,355 and $75,937.

The combination of extreme oversold readings and strong downward momentum leaves room for a temporary bounce, but not enough evidence to declare a bottom.

For now, traders face two major macroeconomic checkpoints: the Fed's November 18 meeting minutes and the November 25 PCE inflation report, both of which could influence expectations ahead of December's interest-rate decision.

#4969. Bitcoin ETFs lose $1 billion for the second week in a row as crypto funds, except one, continue bleeding

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The 12 U.S. spot bitcoin funds have lost $1.91 billion over seven straight trading days, and no other crypto ETF categories, save one, saw any net inflows last week.

U.S. spot bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) ETFs saw $1.07 billion in net outflows last week, their second straight week with more than $1 billion leaving the funds, per The Block's analysis of SoSoValue data. The last time the funds posted back-to-back $1 billion outflow weeks was in late May and early June.

The selling stretched to nearly every crypto ETF category. Of the 15 groups of U.S. spot crypto funds tracked by SoSoValue, 10 posted net outflows last week and four reported no flows at all. Avalanche Avalanche (AVAX) funds were the only category with a weekly inflow, taking in a minute $227,000 on Thursday. Overall, U.S. spot crypto ETFs saw about $1.55 billion in total leave the funds.

The bitcoin funds saw outflows in all five days last week. They lost $201.1 million on Monday, $95 million on Tuesday, $299.9 million on Wednesday, $284 million on Thursday and $185.5 million on Friday.

Combined with the $1.28 billion that left the funds the week before, bitcoin ETFs have now shed $2.35 billion over two weeks. That is the largest two-week total since the fortnight ending June 5, when the funds lost $3.14 billion.

Friday's outflow was the bitcoin funds' seventh consecutive daily loss, a losing streak that has drained $1.91 billion from the funds since it began Nov. 5. It is the longest daily outflow streak since the 10-session stretch from June 17 to July 1, which drained about $2.71 billion, as The Block reported at the time.

BlackRock's IBIT accounted for $143.5 million of Friday's outflows, or about 77% of the total, per SoSoValue. Fidelity's FBTC lost $41.9 million, and the other 10 funds reported no flows. IBIT currently holds bitcoin worth $53.99 billion against $64.19 billion in cumulative inflows since launch.

Bitcoin ETFs have come to lose $2.35 billion in November after nine trading days, already their largest monthly outflow since June, when $4.51 billion left the funds. They are now down about $1.98 billion for 2026, more than double the $914.1 million deficit they carried a week earlier after flipping negative for the year.

The outflows came as bitcoin dropped below $69,000 early Friday, its lowest level since Aug. 20 at the time, as traders weighed Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike, as The Block reported. The world's most valuable cryptocurrency fell further on Saturday morning, currently trading around $65,650, per The Block's Bitcoin price page.

Spot ether Ethereum (ETH) ETFs lost $398.9 million last week, per SoSoValue, their seventh consecutive negative week; the category has twice posted eight-week outflow streaks, most recently when it matched that record in early July, so another negative week would tie it again.

The seven-week losing streak has pulled about $2.42 billion from the funds since late September, per SoSoValue's data. Monday's $184.5 million outflow was last week's largest, followed by $144.8 million on Wednesday and $70.6 million on Thursday.

A minuscule $2.4 million inflow on Friday ended a six-trading-day outflow streak worth $594.4 million. Fidelity's FETH drew $11.6 million that day, offsetting a $9.3 million outflow from Grayscale's Ethereum Mini Trust, while BlackRock's ETHA reported no flows.

Ether ETFs are now down about $804.5 million for 2026, nearly double the $405.6 million deficit from a week earlier. Net assets fell 15.5% over the week to $10.85 billion, their lowest since Aug. 18 and about $670 million below the funds' $11.52 billion in cumulative net inflows.

Spot Solana ETFs lost $32.1 million last week, per SoSoValue, their sixth straight negative week and the longest such run since the funds launched in October 2025. The outflow streak began the same week the funds snapped a record 14-week inflow run, and it has drained $197.4 million since.

The Solana funds posted outflows in every session last week, extending their daily losing streak to seven days. Fidelity's FSOL accounted for all of Friday's $3.1 million outflow. Net assets fell to $1.14 billion from $1.31 billion a week earlier, though, unlike their BTC and ETH brethren, the funds remain about $644.1 million positive for the year.

Grayscale's Zcash fund, ZCSH, the only U.S. spot Zcash ETF, lost $30.7 million, nearly as much as the nine Solana funds combined, per SoSoValue. It was the fund's second straight negative week, and the outflow matched an early-October week as its largest since late September. ZCSH's net assets fell 32% over the week to $523.7 million.

Spot XRP ETFs shed $19.1 million, per SoSoValue, their largest weekly outflow since mid-March and a second straight negative week. Most of it left on Monday and Tuesday, at $10.4 million and $7.6 million, respectively. On Friday, Grayscale's GXRP lost $5.5 million while Franklin's XRPZ took in $4.5 million.

The three U.S. Hyperliquid ETFs lost $4.3 million, extending their weekly outflow streak to six, the longest since they began trading in May, per SoSoValue. Smaller funds tracking NEAR, Chainlink, Hedera and Polkadot lost between $99,000 and $1.4 million each. The BNB, Dogecoin, Tron and Litecoin funds reported no flows for the week.

The Avalanche funds’ modest $227,000 inflow on Thursday, their only day with any net flows, formed the only black in a sea of red last week.

#4967. Emideltide Keeps Getting a ‘No’ for Compounding. What’s the Problem?

Why the government’s renewed interest in peptides excludes this one.

THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION has not been shy about its pro-peptide stance. US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has pushed to make six popular yet unapproved peptides available for compounding to people with a prescription. A recent FDA advisory committee meeting voted in favor of adding six out of seven peptides to a list of substances that U.S. compounding pharmacies are allowed to manufacture and supply.

Six out of seven. So what happened to that last peptide? Emideltide, also dubbed DSIP, is a peptide people have turned to for better sleep. And it was the only peptide the FDA advisory board voted against moving out of the Category 2 list—a substance considered to carry significant safety risks, with compounding pharmacies prohibited from making it. Here’s why.

EMIDELTIDE IS A nine-amino-acid peptide originally isolated from the blood of sleeping rabbits during electrically induced sleep in the late 1970s. Since its discovery, a synthetic peptide version has been administered via injection or a nasal spray.

Emideltide reportedly helps you fall asleep faster and extend the time spent in deep sleep. It’s also been used to avoid waking up multiple times throughout the night and anecdotal reports online have mentioned more vivid, Inception–like lucid dreaming. With better sleep, people online using emideltide have mentioned feeling less stress, more refreshed upon waking, and faster recovery after a grueling workout.

MOST RESEARCH LOOKING into the peptide’s role in sleep, however, took place in the 1980s and 1990s—with mixed findings.

For example, a 1984 case study reported on a 35-year-old guy with 10 years of narcolepsy who had reduced sleep attacks, less daytime napping, and more alertness with weekly emideltide injections administered in the morning.

One clinical trial had 16 people take an emideltide injection or a placebo while measuring how long it took for them to fall asleep once they’re tucked into bed. People who had an emideltide injection said they felt more tired and actually went to sleep quicker than the placebo group. That should be great except when they repeated the experiment a second night, the placebo group knocked out quicker than the peptide group.

Another study in 1992 found the peptide helped chronic insomniacs feel less tired. However, there was such little difference in the time it took to fall asleep and stay asleep in the emideltide group versus the placebo group. The authors of the 1992 study said any small improvements with the peptide were probably “due to an incidental change in the placebo group” and “not likely to be of major therapeutic benefit.”

BEYOND SLEEP, EMIDELTIDE has been explored in animal studies for potentially protecting against cancer and improving motor ability after stroke. Another realm of interest is how emideltide might help with curbing withdrawal after addiction.

A 1984 study found emideltide injections helped reduce the severity of opioid withdrawal symptoms in 97 percent of people with addiction along with alcohol withdrawal symptoms in 87 percent of people with alcohol addiction. Although more peptide injections were needed in people with opiate addiction.

In 1998, researchers gave a single injection of emideltide to seven people with opioid dependence. While they reported improvements in opioid withdrawal, the team also noted “it remains an open question whether DSIP could be an effective alternative detoxification approach.” Some of the issues were the small sample size, lack of a placebo group for proper comparison, and that each person knew they were getting an emideltide injection. The lack of randomization makes it hard to say for sure that a treatment actually worked or if people subjectively felt better because they knew they were getting treatment.

WE KNOW EMIDELTIDE doesn’t act like a sedative that slows down the brain and body’s function. But how the peptide exactly works is still up for debate.

The peptide is often considered a sleep-regulator rather than a suppressant. We know emideltide doesn’t act like a sedative or sleeping pill that slows down the brain and body’s function. But how the peptide exactly works is still up for debate.

One possible mechanism is that the peptide increases delta-wave activity. These are your slowest brain waves at 0.5 to 4 Hz that are indicative of deep sleep. Deep sleep is linked to better memory, energy, and all that good stuff you get from a good night’s sleep. There may also be some neuroendocrine effects going on that could explain why people feel calm enough to pass out. A small study back in the ’80s injected a single dose of emideltide in 11 guys and found lower levels of ACTH, a hormone that stimulates your adrenal glands to release the stress hormone cortisol (though this mechanism has been disputed).

The FDA advisory meeting relied on studies that focused on emideltide’s cross-talk with the opioid system in the brain. While the peptide doesn’t directly interact with opioid receptors, evidence points to emideltide somehow being able to trigger the release of endorphins. This may also provide painkiller properties (which is why it’s been proposed as a way to suppress alcohol and opioid withdrawal syndrome).

EMIDELTIDE WILL PROBABLY stay banned—and found only through the sketchy gray market—because there’s not enough information to know if emideltide might do more harm than good.

Since emideltide interacts with the opioid system, there is a possibility that it could lead to addiction. Right now, there are no animal or human studies that prove emideltide wouldn’t worsen addictive behaviors.

There’s also not enough data on whether repeated emideltide use would cause other safety issues. While the small sleep trials did not report any serious side effects, withdrawal studies noted headaches, nausea, and vertigo. After the second injection, some had low blood pressure although the researchers also said it’s unclear whether those symptoms were because of the peptide or from withdrawal altogether.

#4966. Louisiana AG calls CFTC chair an ‘obsequious standard bearer’ for prediction markets following agency lawsuit

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The CFTC sued Louisiana on Friday, a day after a state judge ordered Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase, Robinhood and dozens of affiliated entities to stop offering event contracts in the state.

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill accused Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Michael Selig of making "flatly false statements" on Saturday, a day after the agency sued the state to block a court order shutting prediction markets out of Louisiana.

"Flatly false statements by the 'obsequious standard bearer' for Kalshi and prediction markets. Gambling has been regulated by states for 250 years," Murrill wrote on X at 12:05 p.m. ET.

Murrill was replying to a Friday evening post in which Selig said event contracts "have traded openly in Louisiana for years, in compliance with the CEA and [CFTC] regulations." He called the state's "eleventh-hour 'emergency' lawsuit" against the industry "naked lawfare and a cynical political stunt."

"Under the Court’s logic, contracts such as interest rate swaps and weather derivatives, both of which are commonly traded financial instruments that the Louisiana economy is highly dependent on, are illegal gambling products," a Kalshi spokesperson told The Block. "Nothing could better illustrate why Congress gave the CFTC exclusive jurisdiction over our national financial markets."

"Prediction markets are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission under a federal framework, not a patchwork of state rules," a Polymarket spokesperson told The Block.

The CFTC and the United States filed a complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana on Friday, naming the state, Murrill, the Louisiana Gaming Control Board and the state police's gaming enforcement division as defendants. The agency is asking the court to declare that state gambling laws are preempted for CFTC-regulated markets and to bar Louisiana from enforcing or extending the state court's order.

"The Commission's lawsuit seeks to maintain the status quo while the federal courts decide this issue in an orderly manner," Selig said in a statement. The agency said Louisiana is the 12th state it has sued to defend its claimed exclusive jurisdiction over derivatives markets.

On Thursday, the CFTC and the Justice Department also sued Arkansas to block its enforcement action against Kalshi. Selig told a conference audience on Friday that states were "essentially trying to lock up founders and CEOs" of prediction market companies, The Block reported.

Judge Jeffrey Johnson of the 21st Judicial District Court in Tangipahoa Parish signed the ex parte temporary restraining order Thursday afternoon, according to a copy Murrill posted on X. Murrill sued the companies earlier that day, making Louisiana the 11th state to sue one or more prediction markets.

The order names 31 entities tied to Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood, Crypto.com, Coinbase, Gemini, Interactive Brokers' ForecastEx, Novig, Underdog, IG Group and ProphetX. It bars them from offering event contracts on sports, elections, awards and other events to people in Louisiana without a state license, and requires them to geofence the state.

The order expires after 10 days unless the court extends it. A hearing on the state's motion for a preliminary injunction is set for 9 a.m. local time on Nov. 30.

Kalshi has cut off access for Louisiana users. A message in its app, seen in a screenshot reviewed by The Block, tells them, "Your government says you can't use Kalshi anymore," and says the state acted "without a hearing, notice, or due process." The screen includes a link reading "Protect your freedom to trade" and a button to "Join the movement."

The Block has reached out to Polymarket and Murrill's office for comment.

Updated at 4:45 p.m. ET with a statement from Kalshi and at 5:20 p.m. ET with a statement from Polymarket.

#4965. Trump’s First Democratic Picks for SEC and CFTC Could Reshape Crypto’s Regulators

Trump’s First Democratic Picks for SEC and CFTC Could Reshape Crypto’s Regulators

President Donald Trump has nominated four people to fill vacant seats at the two federal agencies writing the rules for crypto, in a bipartisan slate that could reshape the commissions that have increasingly taken the lead on digital-asset policy after Congress stalled.

The White House said Thursday it sent the nominations to the Senate: Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and Kristin Johnson and Steven Levine for the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Each requires Senate confirmation. Notably, the slate pairs a Republican and a Democrat at each agency, with Anonick and Levine the Republicans and Rowland and Johnson the Democrats, marking the first time the administration has put forward Democratic nominees for either commission.

The appointments matter because of how depleted both agencies have become. The CFTC in particular has been running on a skeleton crew, operating with Michael Selig as its lone Senate-confirmed member after a wave of departures, even as it has pursued one of the most aggressive crypto agendas in its history.

Filling those seats would give the commissions the quorum and staying power to turn proposals into durable rules.

Both CFTC nominees come from the Senate Agriculture Committee, which shares jurisdiction over crypto market structure and will vet their nominations. Anonick, a Republican, is legislative counsel to committee Chairman John Boozman and was a lead negotiator on the panel’s portion of the Clarity Act, the crypto market-structure bill that collapsed in the Senate this fall.

Rowland, a Democrat, is a career CFTC attorney detailed to the committee who also worked on the Clarity Act and an earlier 2024 crypto bill. His enforcement-heavy background and party lean could introduce a dissenting voice to a commission that, under Selig, has leaned firmly pro-industry.

On the SEC side, which the Senate Banking Committee will review, the picks would replace two commissioners central to crypto policy in opposite ways. Levine, a Republican, is slated to fill the seat of Hester Peirce, the agency’s most prominent crypto advocate and the head of its Crypto Task Force.

Levine’s own views on digital assets are not well established publicly, making his future votes a key variable for whether the SEC’s crypto-friendly push holds.

Johnson, a Democrat and former CFTC commissioner, would take the seat of frequent crypto skeptic Caroline Crenshaw; at the CFTC she focused on digital-asset custody and DeFi and pressed for stronger customer protections and conflict-of-interest rules.

The timing underscores a shift following the collapse of the Clarity Act, the crypto industry’s marquee market structure bill that would have established more-favorable-than-not rules for most of crypto.

After the legislation failed to advance in the Senate, the SEC and CFTC moved to fill the vacuum with their own authority, leaving the industry to get its “clarity” from regulators rather than legislators. A fully staffed pair of commissions would cement that dynamic.

Those agency efforts have been sweeping: The CFTC has cleared perpetual futures on individual stocks, floated bringing crypto exchanges under federal oversight, and moved to define event contracts as “swaps.” The SEC, meanwhile, rolled out an “innovation exemption” for tokenized stocks, proposed rules letting investment advisers custody crypto, and issued guidance suggesting most crypto assets aren’t securities.

The nominations are the first Trump has sent for these seats in roughly a year, a gap that reflected turbulence around crypto appointments. The administration previously pulled its CFTC chair nominee, Brian Quintenz, amid a clash involving the Winklevoss twins.

The confirmation window is now tight: with the Senate heading toward Democratic control in January, Republicans have only a short lame-duck stretch to move the slate before the calculus changes.

#4962. Strategy stock sheds 5% amid MSCI index removal, Bitcoin sell-off

Strategy shares declined Thursday following MSCI’s decision to remove the company from its indexes, as Bitcoin also fell amid a broader crypto market decline.

Shares of Michael Saylor’s Bitcoin treasury company Strategy fell 6.49% on Thursday, closing at $114.41, a day after MSCI confirmed the company’s removal from its global equity indexes and amid a broader cryptocurrency market sell-off.

On Wednesday, MSCI confirmed that Strategy would be removed from its global equity indexes after the Nov. 30 market close, a move that could trigger selling by funds tracking the benchmarks. JPMorgan previously estimated that the exclusion could result in roughly $2.8 billion in selling pressure.

Ryan Kirkley, CEO of Global Settlement Network, told Cointelegraph that MSCI’s decision could help distinguish Bitcoin treasury companies from traditional operating businesses and limit indirect cryptocurrency exposure for passive investors.

“Index inclusion meant ordinary passive investors, like someone holding a global index fund in their pension, were getting leveraged Bitcoin exposure they never chose. MSCI just fixed that,” he said.

Kirkley added that MSCI’s decision also raises broader questions about whether Bitcoin treasury companies should be classified alongside traditional operating businesses.

In its Aug. 31 response to MSCI’s proposed rules, Strategy argued that the changes were a pretext for targeting digital asset treasury companies. It also downplayed the potential financial impact, saying MSCI-linked funds held approximately 13 million of its shares, representing just 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding.

The stock’s decline coincided with a broader cryptocurrency market sell-off. Bitcoin traded near $71,340 as of 4:08 p.m. ET on Thursday, down 4.3% over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGecko data. The total cryptocurrency market capitalization declined 3% to around $2.49 trillion.

#4961. Kava Lend loses roughly $3.8 million to hack, sending KAVA token down nearly 40%

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Onchain data shows an attacker borrowed out nearly all of Kava Lend's KAVA, worth about $3.76 million before the attack, then bridged most of it to BNB Chain and sold it for roughly $2.1 million.

An attacker drained about 55.2 million KAVA tokens from Kava Lend, the native lending protocol of Layer 1 blockchain Kava (KAVA), late Friday after inflating the value of deposits in a dormant stablecoin market and borrowing against them, according to onchain data reviewed by The Block.

The tokens were worth roughly $3.76 million at the $0.068 price KAVA traded at before the attack. Kava Lend's module account, where the protocol's pooled deposits sit, went from holding 55.33 million KAVA to 0.19 KAVA in a little over an hour and a half.

"We are tracking unexpected behavior originating from a dApp within the Kava ecosystem," Kava wrote on X at 6:28 a.m. ET on Saturday in its first public acknowledgment of the incident, more than seven hours after the attack started.

In a follow-up post about half an hour later, Kava said it was aware of "the bridging and sale of KAVA tokens on BSC." "To clarify: This is not an infinite mint," the team wrote. "The event is isolated and contained within Kava Lend."

Kava hasn't put an official number on the losses or published a post-mortem report of the attack.

The exploit ran through Kava Lend's market for BUSD, the Binance-branded stablecoin that issuer Paxos stopped minting in 2023. The market was all but empty ahead of the attack, onchain data shows.

Kava Lend works out what depositors have earned by dividing the interest borrowers pay by the market's net supply, per Kava's public source code. The code skips the division if that supply figure is exactly zero; however, it doesn't check for figures that are minute, but still above zero.

At 11:01 p.m. ET on Friday, the attacker used a small BUSD loan to bring the market's net supply down to two hundred-millionths of a dollar. Over the next three minutes, Kava Lend multiplied the value of every BUSD deposit roughly 243,000-fold. That included BUSD the attacker had deposited ahead of time, which the protocol now counted as roughly 1.25 billion BUSD in collateral.

The attacker then borrowed KAVA against their deposit 127 times, using a second account to clear each loan and get around Kava Lend's cap on KAVA borrowing. The attacker appears to have prepared for at least a week, running repeated deposit and borrow cycles in the BUSD market from Nov. 8.

Beginning at 4:59 a.m. ET on Saturday, the attacker bridged about 49.2 million KAVA to an address on BNB Chain through Kava's LayerZero bridge. Most of it was sold within the hour for 3,006.5 BNB and 231,557 USDT, worth about $2.09 million combined, and the BNB has since been moved out. Another roughly 4.58 million KAVA went to five unlabeled addresses on Kava.

KAVA was trading near $0.042 at time of publication, down about 39% over the past 24 hours, according to The Block's Kava Price page. Partner exchanges paused deposits and withdrawals "as a standard precautionary measure," Kava said.

At 9:05 a.m. ET, Kava said it had paused the Axelar bridge "out of an abundance of caution," though the drained KAVA left the network through LayerZero. "We will share a complete incident report as soon as it is ready," the team wrote.

The Kava incident follows several lending protocol exploits this year where an attacker borrowed against collateral worth far less than the protocol believed. Cronos halted its network in August after an exploit of lending protocol Tectonic estimated at $75 million, and Hedera's Bonzo Lend was hit for roughly $9 million in July.
